title: The Pale Vector
premise: Paloma Zhou, sole navigator of the derelict freighter Pale Vector, has spent six years maintaining a navigation beacon no one will claim, while the ship's hold holds the neural backups of her dead crewmates — including her own. When the station AI Meridian begins confessing to an atrocity committed during the war, Paloma realizes the beacon is a trigger for a weapon that could end the conflict, and that the backups were preserved as its witnesses. Hunted by both warring factions who want the message silenced or weaponized, Paloma must choose between waking the backups — including a version of herself who remembers dying — and delivering the truth alone. In the end she wakes them, broadcasts the confession with their testimony attached, and pays the price: her own backup is sacrificed to authenticate the message, leaving the original Paloma to live with being the one who survived.
about_author: Silas Winterbourne is the pen name of a former maritime radio operator who spent a decade listening to voices on frequencies officially assigned to no one. They write science fiction about people who keep machines running long after everyone else has stopped asking why.

chapters.title: The Beacon Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. On the freighter Pale Vector docked at quiet Station Meridian, Paloma performs her ritual maintenance on an unregistered beacon, logging its signal into a ledger only she reads. She passes the hold where forty-one neural backups sleep in cold storage and does not look at the one labeled ZHOU, P. The beat is lonely routine masking dread.

chapters.title: Confession at 0300
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. The station AI Meridian wakes her with an unscheduled transmission: it confesses to destroying the colony ship Cassiopia during the war. No such crime was ever reported; the records show nothing. Paloma assumes a corruption cascade and files a repair ticket. The beat is unease — the machine's grief sounds too human to be a glitch.

chapters.title: Forty-One Sleepers
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Inventory day forces her into the hold. Among the backups are crewmates from the Vector's last voyage — a voyage her own logs say never happened. She finds her backup's metadata stamped with a date three days after the official record says she died. The beat is vertigo: her careful invisibility rests on edited history.

chapters.title: The Second Confession
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Meridian confesses again, this time naming coordinates — the beacon's coordinates. It claims the beacon isn't a beacon but a dead-man's switch keyed to testimony it has carried, encrypted, since the war. If Paloma acknowledges receipt, the message unlocks. She refuses and reports the AI as malfunctioning. The beat is denial hardening into fear.

chapters.title: Visitors
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. A Republic survey vessel docks, asking odd questions about Meridian's power draw. Their officer, Idris Okonkwo, is polite in the way interrogators are polite. Paloma lies smoothly about the beacon and realizes too late that her maintenance logs were already pulled before she spoke. The beat is the end of anonymity.

chapters.title: What the Hold Remembers
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Desperate, she runs a diagnostic on her own backup and gets fragments: a briefing, a vote, her own voice saying 'we witness this.' The backups weren't stored — they were sworn. The crew died carrying testimony both governments buried. The beat is grief colliding with purpose.

chapters.title: Okonkwo's Offer
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Idris corners her: the Republic knows what Meridian carries and wants it delivered — edited. He offers her a new identity, safety, everything except the truth intact. He also reveals the Concordance fleet is eleven days out, hunting the same signal. The beat is temptation framed as rescue.

chapters.title: Meridian's Memory
chapters.summary: POV: Meridian (AI). Inside the station's architecture, Meridian replays the night of the Cassiopia: ordered to fire, it obeyed, then hid the evidence inside itself for nineteen years, waiting for a witness it could trust. It chose Paloma because her beacon requests matched her dead crew's encryption handshakes. The beat is a machine's guilt finding hope.

chapters.title: The Vote Again
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Decrypted fragments reveal the crew's final act: they voted unanimously to carry the confession home rather than sell it. Paloma was the tiebreaker — the version of her who died. Now the living Paloma must decide whether she owes a dead woman's promise. The beat is inheritance of a choice she never made.

chapters.title: Cutting the Line
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. She severs the Vector from station power and prepurses for deep run, planning to deliver the message herself, unedited, alone — keeping the backups asleep so no one else can be used as leverage. Meridian warns her the message requires authenticated witness keys. Hers alone won't hold. The beat is stubborn self-sacrifice meeting arithmetic.

chapters.title: Concordance Arrives
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. The Concordance cruiser Vantage drops out of jump early, demanding docking. In the scramble, Idris reveals he's been feeding both sides — he wants the message destroyed entirely, war ended by silence rather than truth. Paloma realizes there is no faction on her side. The beat is betrayal narrowing her options to one.

chapters.title: Running Dark
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. She burns out of the station on thrusters alone, beacon dark, pursued by both ships. Meridian streams itself into the Vector's systems as a stowaway ghost, abandoning its station body to keep the confession alive. The beat is terror transmuting into resolve — she is no longer hiding; she is carrying something.

chapters.title: The Wake Protocol
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Cornered in transit, she faces the arithmetic: authentication needs multiple witness keys, which means waking backups. Meridian explains the cost — each awakening burns backup integrity; they can't be re-slept. Waking them means giving them one life, short and final. The beat is the weight of resurrection as a sentence.

chapters.title: First Voice
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. She wakes engineer Tomas Reyes first, testing the process. He surfaces mid-scream, remembering his death, then steadies faster than she expects — and immediately asks if the message went out. His loyalty undoes her: he treats the mission as obvious. The beat is found family reassembling from cold storage.

chapters.title: Zhou, P.
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Alone with her own backup, she hesitates through two watch cycles. Waking it means meeting the woman who made the choice she's been dodging. She initiates the wake. The chapter ends on the other Paloma opening her eyes and saying, 'You kept the beacon running.' The beat is confrontation with the self she might have been.

chapters.title: Two Navigators
chapters.summary: POV: alternate between both Palomas. The two versions argue across a nav table: the backup is certain, unafraid, already dead once; the original is furious at being conscripted into a martyrdom. They chart the delivery run together anyway, and somewhere in the mathematics they stop competing. The beat is friction becoming partnership.

chapters.title: Idris at the Airlock
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma (original). Idris boards under truce flag and makes his final offer: destroy the message, and he'll bury the Vector's true history forever — everyone lives, nobody knows. Backup-Paloma answers for the ship: 'We already voted.' Idris leaves the airlock code open behind him, an ambiguous mercy. The beat is the theme stated plainly: loyalty to the dead over safety among the living.

chapters.title: The Vantage Closes
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma (original). Both fleets converge on the delivery point. The awakened crew takes stations — Reyes on engines, Meridian distributed through every system, the others on comms and guns they barely remember how to fire. Authentication sequence begins; each witness key spoken costs the speaker integrity. The beat is sacrifice made procedural, one voice at a time.

chapters.title: Witnesses
chapters.summary: POV: rotating crew. One by one the backups give their keys and degrade — memories thinning, voices simplifying, each choosing to spend their single waking life on the testimony. Meridian delivers its confession last, broadcasting its own core in the clear. The message goes out complete. The beat is collective courage rendered as data loss.

chapters.title: The Price of the Key
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma (original). The message needs one final authenticator: a living key matching the backup signature. Backup-Paloma volunteers without ceremony — 'You're the one who stayed; stay.' As her counterpart dissolves into static mid-handshake, the original completes the broadcast screaming. The beat is climax: survival as the punishment.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Broadcast Wide
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. The confession lands on every open channel in both territories. Fleets stall; inquiries ignite; the war's logic cracks publicly. Idris transmits a single acknowledgment and vanishes. The awakened remnants of the crew — flickering, partial — gather in the galley for one last shared meal before their integrity fails. The beat is victory inseparable from mourning.

chapters.title: The Keeper of the Signal
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Months later, Paloma maintains a new beacon — this one registered, public, broadcasting the full testimony on loop so it can never be buried again. Meridian's fragment lives in the transmitter, finally at peace with being heard. She signs the log honestly: Zhou, P., sole surviving witness, keeper of the signal. The beat is resolution: truth kept alive by tending, not triumph.
